pages.body:
Fill a clear cup with water and leave it on a windowsill in the sun for two days. Do not cover it. Check on it each day and write down what you notice about the water level.

- Where do you think the water goes?
- Have you ever noticed water droplets forming on the inside of a cold drink bottle, or on a cooking pot lid? Where do you think that water came from?

Water is always moving between the earth and the sky. It moves in a set order of stages, and once the last stage is complete, the whole journey starts again. Scientists call this repeated journey the water cycle.

[[img:ibf8xd970]]

| **Stage** | **What happens** |
|---|---|
| Evaporation | The sun heats water in seas, rivers and lakes. The water turns into water vapour, an invisible gas, and rises into the air. |
| Transpiration | Plants also lose water vapour into the air through their leaves. This adds to the water vapour rising from evaporation. |
| Condensation | As the water vapour rises, it cools down. It changes back into tiny droplets of water, which gather together to form clouds. |
| Precipitation | When the droplets in a cloud become too heavy to stay in the air, they fall back to earth as rain. In very cold places, this may fall as snow or hail instead. |
| Collection or run off | The water that falls collects in seas, rivers, lakes and underground. From there, the whole cycle begins again. |

questions.q: Name the five stages of the water cycle in the correct order.

parts.a: Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and collection or run off.

questions.q: What causes water to evaporate from the sea?

parts.a: The heat of the sun.

questions.q: Explain, in your own words, why clouds form.

parts.a: As water vapour rises it cools and changes back into tiny droplets of water. The droplets gather together to form clouds.

ideas.t: It condenses into tiny droplets that gather to form clouds

questions.q: Name the five stages of the water cycle in order.

parts.a: Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and collection or run off.

questions.q: What is the difference between evaporation and transpiration?

parts.a: Evaporation is water turning to vapour from seas, rivers and lakes heated by the sun. Transpiration is water vapour lost from the leaves of plants.

ideas.t: Evaporation is liquid water from seas, rivers and lakes heated by the sun turning to vapour
Transpiration is water vapour lost through the leaves of plants

questions.q: Explain what happens during condensation.

parts.a: The water vapour rises and cools. It changes back into tiny droplets of liquid water, which gather to form clouds.

ideas.t: It changes back into tiny droplets of liquid water (clouds)

questions.q: You place a lid over a pot of boiling water. After a few minutes, you notice water droplets on the underside of the lid. Explain which stage of the water cycle this represents, and why it happens.

parts.a: This is condensation. The water vapour rising from the boiling water meets the cooler lid, cools down and changes back into droplets of water.

ideas.t: The vapour cools on the cooler lid and turns back into droplets of water

questions.q: A region has very few trees because of heavy deforestation. Suggest how this might affect the amount of transpiration in the area, and what effect this could have on local rainfall.

parts.a: With fewer trees there is less transpiration, so less water vapour is added to the air. Less vapour means fewer clouds and less rainfall in the area.

ideas.t: Less water vapour goes into the air
So fewer clouds form and there is less rainfall

parts.q: Name the five stages of the water cycle in the correct order.
parts.a: Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and collection or run off.

parts.q: Choose one stage and explain what happens during it.
parts.a: For example, condensation: water vapour cools and changes back into tiny droplets that form clouds.

parts.q: Explain two ways the water cycle benefits your community.
parts.a: It provides clean water for drinking and carries nutrients to farmland.

ideas.t: Improves the water table (wells and boreholes)

parts.q: Suggest one thing your community could do to protect its water sources so the water cycle continues to provide clean water.
parts.a: For example, keep rivers and streams clean, avoid dumping waste in water, or plant trees.

ideas.t: Gives a sensible way to protect water sources

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What happens to rain after it falls

pages.body:
> **The water cycle has no start and no end. It is a pattern that repeats again and again.**

## What happens to rain after it falls

Rain that reaches the ground follows different paths. Some flows over the surface as runoff and joins streams and rivers, which carry it to lakes and the sea. Some soaks into the soil, which is called infiltration. Water that sinks deeper collects underground as groundwater, and the top of this underground water is called the water table. Plants take up part of the water through their roots and release it to the air as water vapour by transpiration.

The natural sources of water are rain, rivers, streams, lakes, springs, the sea and groundwater. People reach groundwater through wells and boreholes.

questions.q: What is runoff?

parts.a: Runoff is rain water that flows over the surface of the ground and joins streams and rivers, which carry it to lakes and the sea.

ideas.t: Water flows over the ground surface
Joins streams, rivers, lakes or the sea

questions.q: What is the water table?

parts.a: The water table is the top of the water that has collected underground as groundwater.

questions.q: Name four natural sources of water.

parts.a: Any four of: rain, rivers, streams, lakes, springs, the sea and groundwater.

questions.q: A community borehole gives less water at the end of a long dry season. Use your knowledge of groundwater to explain why.

parts.a: In the long dry season there is no rain to soak into the ground and refill the groundwater. The water table falls, so the borehole reaches less water.

ideas.t: No rain in the dry season
Water table falls so less water

pages.body:
Imagine your town did not receive rain for two whole years. Think about everything in your community that depends on rain or on a steady supply of clean water.

- List as many things as you can think of that would be affected.
- Which of these do you think would be affected first?

The water cycle is not just an interesting pattern in nature. It supports life on earth in several important ways.

| **Why it matters** | **Explanation** |
|---|---|
| Provides clean water | As water evaporates, it leaves behind salt, dirt and other impurities. The water that falls as rain is naturally cleaned, giving us fresh water to drink and use. |
| Carries nutrients | Moving water picks up and carries nutrients from the soil and rocks, spreading them to rivers, farmland and the sea, where plants and animals depend on them. |
| Improves the water table | Rain that soaks into the ground refills the underground water that feeds wells and boreholes. |
| Regulates weather patterns | The movement of water and the energy it carries help to control temperature and rainfall patterns across regions. |
| Releases energy | Evaporation absorbs heat, and condensation releases it back into the surroundings. This exchange of energy helps to warm and cool the environment. |
> **Without the water cycle, we would have no rain, no rivers, and no fresh water to drink.**

questions.q: Name three reasons why the water cycle is important to your community.

parts.a: It provides clean water, carries nutrients, improves the water table, regulates weather patterns and releases energy.

ideas.t: Improves the water table (wells and boreholes)

questions.q: Explain how the water cycle helps to provide clean drinking water.

parts.a: As water evaporates it leaves salt, dirt and other impurities behind, so the rain that falls is naturally clean fresh water that we can use.

ideas.t: Evaporation leaves salt, dirt and impurities behind
The rain that falls is clean fresh water to drink

questions.q: How does the water cycle affect farming in your community?

parts.a: Rain supplies water for crops, moving water carries nutrients to farmland, and rain that soaks into the ground refills the water table that feeds wells and boreholes.

ideas.t: Refills the water table, wells and boreholes

questions.q: Give two reasons why the water cycle is important.

parts.a: It provides clean water and carries nutrients (also: improves the water table, regulates weather, releases energy).

ideas.t: Improves the water table (wells and boreholes)

questions.q: A farmer notices that a nearby well has been drying up over the past few years, during a time when rainfall in the area has also dropped. Using what you know about the water cycle, explain a possible reason for this.

parts.a: Less rain means less water soaks into the ground, so the water table is not refilled. The water table falls and the well, which depends on it, dries up.

ideas.t: Less rainfall means less water soaks into the ground
The water table is not refilled and falls
So the well that depends on it dries up

pages.body:
- The water cycle is the repeated journey of water between the earth and the sky.
- The five stages are evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, and collection or run off.
- Evaporation and transpiration add water vapour to the air. Condensation turns that vapour into clouds. Precipitation brings the water back down. Collection gathers it, ready for the cycle to begin again.
- The water cycle provides clean water, carries nutrients, improves the water table, regulates weather patterns and releases energy into the environment.
- The water cycle has no beginning and no end. It is a repeated pattern in nature.
- Rain water may run off over the surface, soak into the soil as groundwater or be taken up by plants, so water keeps moving through the water cycle.

| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Water cycle | The repeated journey of water between the earth and the sky |
| Evaporation | The change of water from a liquid into water vapour, caused by heat |
| Water vapour | Water in the form of an invisible gas |
| Transpiration | The loss of water vapour from a plant's leaves into the air |
| Condensation | The change of water vapour back into tiny droplets of liquid water |
| Precipitation | Water falling from clouds to the earth as rain, snow or hail |
| Collection or run off | The gathering of fallen water in seas, rivers, lakes and underground |
| Water table | The level underground below which the soil and rock are full of water |
